_link.title: I can summarise the impact of changing SA:V ratio on the efficiency of cellular functions

toLevel2.stem: As a cell grows larger, what happens to its SA:V ratio?

options.text: It decreases
options.explanation: Volume increases faster than surface area as a cell grows, so the SA:V ratio decreases.

options.text: It increases
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio decreases because volume grows faster than surface area.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio changes as the cell grows; it does not remain constant.

options.text: It doubles in value
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio decreases rather than doubling as the cell grows.

toLevel2.stem: Why does a lower SA:V ratio make exchange less efficient?

options.text: Less membrane surface is available per unit volume for nutrient exchange
options.explanation: With less surface area relative to volume, fewer nutrients and wastes can be exchanged per unit of cell contents.

options.text: The cell membrane becomes thicker and blocks all transport completely
options.explanation: Membrane thickness does not change with cell size; the issue is the ratio of surface to volume.

options.text: The nucleus shrinks and produces fewer instructions for transport proteins
options.explanation: The nucleus does not shrink; the issue is geometric — less surface relative to volume.

options.text: Waste products dissolve the membrane as the cell gets larger over time
options.explanation: Waste does not dissolve the membrane; the problem is insufficient surface for exchange.

toLevel2.stem: What must a cell do when it can no longer sustain itself due to a low SA:V ratio?

options.text: Divide into smaller cells
options.explanation: Dividing restores a higher SA:V ratio, improving the efficiency of exchange for each daughter cell.

options.text: Grow even larger to compensate
options.explanation: Growing larger would further reduce the SA:V ratio and worsen the problem.

options.text: Stop all metabolic activity permanently
options.explanation: Stopping metabolism would kill the cell; division is the solution.

options.text: Merge with a neighbouring cell nearby
options.explanation: Merging would create a larger cell with an even lower SA:V ratio.

toLevel2.stem: Which property increases faster as a cell grows: surface area or volume?

options.text: Volume
options.explanation: Volume increases as the cube of the radius while surface area increases as the square, so volume grows faster.

options.text: Surface area
options.explanation: Surface area increases more slowly than volume as the cell grows.

options.text: Both increase at exactly the same rate
options.explanation: Volume increases faster than surface area due to their different mathematical relationships.

options.text: Neither increases as cells grow
options.explanation: Both increase, but volume increases proportionally faster.

toLevel2.stem: A cell with a SA:V ratio of 6:1 compared to one with 3:1 would be more efficient at what?

options.text: Exchanging materials with its environment
options.explanation: A higher SA:V ratio means more surface area per unit volume, allowing more efficient exchange.

options.text: Storing large amounts of food inside it
options.explanation: A higher SA:V ratio favours exchange efficiency, not storage capacity.

options.text: Resisting damage from external pressure
options.explanation: SA:V ratio relates to exchange efficiency, not structural resistance.

options.text: Moving quickly through its surrounding fluid
options.explanation: SA:V ratio affects exchange efficiency, not motility.

toLevel2.stem: As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Volume increases as the cube while surface area increases as the square, so volume outpaces surface area.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is correct; volume grows faster than surface area.

toLevel2.stem: A high SA:V ratio means the cell has more membrane surface per unit volume for exchange.

options.text: True
options.explanation: A high SA:V ratio indicates more surface area relative to volume, improving exchange efficiency.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is correct; a high SA:V ratio means more surface per unit volume.

toLevel2.stem: As a cell grows, its SA:V ratio {{blank:1}}, making the exchange of nutrients and wastes less {{blank:2}}.

options.text: decreases
options.explanation: Volume grows faster than surface area, reducing the SA:V ratio.

options.text: increases
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio decreases, not increases, as the cell grows.

options.text: stays constant
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio changes as the cell grows; it decreases.

options.text: efficient
options.explanation: Less surface per unit volume means exchange is less efficient.

options.text: frequent
options.explanation: The issue is efficiency of exchange, not how often it occurs.

options.text: dangerous
options.explanation: Exchange itself is not dangerous; a low SA:V ratio makes it less efficient.

toLevel2.stem: When a cell's SA:V ratio becomes too low, it must {{blank:1}} to restore a higher ratio for efficient {{blank:2}}.

options.text: divide
options.explanation: Dividing creates smaller cells with higher SA:V ratios.

options.text: grow larger
options.explanation: Growing larger would reduce the SA:V ratio further.

options.text: stop dividing
options.explanation: Stopping division would not resolve the low SA:V ratio problem.

options.text: exchange
options.explanation: Division restores the SA:V ratio, improving the cell's ability to exchange materials.

options.text: photosynthesis
options.explanation: While photosynthesis occurs in some cells, the SA:V issue relates to general material exchange.

options.text: reproduction
options.explanation: Division is the process, not the purpose; the goal is efficient exchange.

toLevel2.stem: A cell with a SA:V ratio of 6:1 has {{blank:1}} units of surface for every unit of {{blank:2}}.

options.text: six
options.explanation: A ratio of 6:1 means six units of surface area for every one unit of volume.

options.text: one
options.explanation: One unit refers to the volume, not the surface area in a 6:1 ratio.

options.text: three
options.explanation: Three would describe a 3:1 ratio, not 6:1.

options.text: volume
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio compares surface area to volume.

options.text: mass
options.explanation: The ratio compares surface area to volume, not mass.

options.text: length
options.explanation: The ratio compares surface area to volume, not length.

toLevel3.stem: Why do large multicellular organisms need specialised organ systems rather than relying on diffusion alone?

options.text: Their overall SA:V ratio is too low for diffusion to supply all cells efficiently
options.explanation: Large organisms have a very low SA:V ratio, so diffusion alone cannot supply nutrients to deep internal cells fast enough.

options.text: Diffusion does not occur in multicellular organisms at all because cells are too close
options.explanation: Diffusion does occur but is insufficient over large distances; organ systems are needed to supplement it.

options.text: Organ systems are simpler than diffusion and require less energy to operate overall
options.explanation: Organ systems are complex and energy-intensive; they are needed because diffusion is too slow over large distances.

options.text: Large organisms have higher SA:V ratios so diffusion is actually faster in them
options.explanation: Large organisms have lower SA:V ratios, which is why they need organ systems.

toLevel3.stem: A small cell has a SA:V ratio of 6:1 and a larger cell has 3:1. Why does the smaller cell exchange materials more efficiently?

options.text: Each unit of volume in the small cell has twice the surface area for exchange
options.explanation: At 6:1, each unit of volume has six units of surface, compared to only three at 3:1, doubling the exchange capacity per volume.

options.text: The small cell has more mitochondria to power active transport across its membrane
options.explanation: The efficiency difference is due to the geometric ratio, not the number of mitochondria.

options.text: The large cell's membrane is thicker, blocking more substances from crossing it
options.explanation: Membrane thickness does not change with cell size; the issue is the SA:V ratio.

options.text: The small cell produces more ATP per unit volume than the larger cell can produce
options.explanation: While energy production matters, the key factor here is the geometric SA:V ratio.

toLevel3.stem: Why is the SA:V ratio the reason cells are typically small?

options.text: Small cells maintain a high SA:V ratio needed for efficient exchange of materials
options.explanation: Remaining small keeps the SA:V ratio high, ensuring enough surface area for the cell to exchange nutrients and wastes.

options.text: Small cells are easier for the organism to move around within its body systems
options.explanation: Cell size is limited by the SA:V ratio and exchange efficiency, not by ease of movement.

options.text: Large cells would be too heavy for the cytoskeleton to support their internal weight
options.explanation: Weight is not the primary limiting factor; exchange efficiency due to SA:V ratio is.

options.text: Small cells can hide from predators more easily than large cells in the environment
options.explanation: Predator avoidance is not the reason for cell size limits; SA:V ratio is the key factor.

toLevel3.stem: How does cell division solve the problem of a decreasing SA:V ratio?

options.text: It produces two smaller cells each with a higher SA:V ratio than the original
options.explanation: Dividing the cell creates smaller daughter cells with more surface area relative to their volume.

options.text: It increases the total volume of the organism without changing surface area at all
options.explanation: Division creates smaller cells; the SA:V ratio of each individual cell increases.

options.text: It removes excess cytoplasm that was blocking exchange across the cell membrane
options.explanation: The issue is geometric, not about cytoplasm blockage; division restores a favourable ratio.

options.text: It creates new membrane proteins that speed up transport regardless of cell size
options.explanation: While new proteins are made, the key benefit is the improved SA:V ratio of smaller cells.

toLevel3.stem: Why do nutrients take longer to reach the centre of a large cell compared to a small cell?

options.text: The greater distance from the membrane to the centre slows diffusion delivery
options.explanation: In a large cell, the centre is farther from the membrane, so it takes longer for nutrients to diffuse to internal regions.

options.text: Large cells have fewer transport proteins on their membrane surface than small cells
options.explanation: The issue is the distance nutrients must travel, not the number of transport proteins.

options.text: The cytoplasm in large cells is denser and actively blocks nutrient movement inside
options.explanation: Cytoplasm density does not significantly change with cell size; the issue is diffusion distance.

options.text: Large cells do not have a nucleus so nutrients have no target to reach inside them
options.explanation: Large cells do have a nucleus; the issue is the diffusion distance, not the lack of targets.

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between SA:V ratio and the rate of waste removal from a cell?

options.text: A higher SA:V ratio allows wastes to be removed faster across the membrane
options.explanation: More surface area relative to volume means more membrane is available for waste to diffuse out.

options.text: SA:V ratio has no effect on waste removal because waste leaves through the nucleus
options.explanation: Waste crosses the plasma membrane; a higher SA:V ratio provides more surface for this.

options.text: A lower SA:V ratio improves waste removal because volume pushes waste out of the cell
options.explanation: Lower SA:V ratio means less surface for waste removal, making it less efficient.

options.text: Waste removal depends only on enzymes and is completely unrelated to SA:V ratio values
options.explanation: While enzymes play a role, the rate of waste crossing the membrane depends on available surface area.

toLevel3.stem: Cell division restores a higher SA:V ratio by creating smaller daughter cells.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Smaller cells have a higher SA:V ratio, improving exchange efficiency.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is correct; division creates smaller cells with improved SA:V ratios.

toLevel3.stem: Large organisms need specialised organ systems because their overall SA:V ratio is too {{blank:1}} for {{blank:2}} alone to supply all cells.

options.text: low
options.explanation: Large organisms have a very low SA:V ratio, making surface exchange insufficient.

options.text: high
options.explanation: A high SA:V ratio would make diffusion more efficient, not less.

options.text: variable
options.explanation: The issue is that the ratio is consistently too low, not that it varies.

options.text: diffusion
options.explanation: Diffusion is too slow over large distances to meet the needs of all cells in a large organism.

options.text: osmosis
options.explanation: While osmosis is important, the broader issue is that passive transport (including diffusion) is insufficient.

options.text: mitosis
options.explanation: Mitosis is cell division, not a mechanism for nutrient supply.

toLevel3.stem: Nutrients take longer to reach the {{blank:1}} of a large cell because the {{blank:2}} from the membrane is greater.

options.text: centre
options.explanation: The centre of a large cell is the farthest point from the membrane surface.

options.text: membrane
options.explanation: Nutrients enter at the membrane; it is the centre they must reach.

options.text: outside
options.explanation: Nutrients start outside; they need to reach the cell's interior.

options.text: diffusion distance
options.explanation: In a larger cell, substances must travel farther from the membrane to reach internal regions.

options.text: membrane thickness
options.explanation: Membrane thickness does not change with cell size; the distance to the centre does.

options.text: number of pores
options.explanation: The issue is the internal distance, not the number of membrane pores.

toLevel3.stem: A higher SA:V ratio means more {{blank:1}} is available per unit of {{blank:2}} for exchanging materials.

options.text: membrane surface
options.explanation: More surface area relative to volume provides more membrane for transport.

options.text: cytoplasm
options.explanation: Cytoplasm is internal; the exchange occurs at the membrane surface.

options.text: nuclear material
options.explanation: Nuclear material is not involved in surface exchange.

options.text: volume
options.explanation: SA:V ratio compares surface area to volume; more surface per volume improves exchange.

options.text: mass
options.explanation: The ratio compares surface area to volume, not mass.

options.text: height
options.explanation: The ratio compares surface area to volume, not height.

toLevel4.stem: A biologist compares two cube-shaped cells: Cell A is 1 cm per side and Cell B is 3 cm per side. Which has a higher SA:V ratio and why?

options.text: Cell A has 6:1 while Cell B has 2:1, because volume grows faster than surface area
options.explanation: Cell A: SA = 6 cm², V = 1 cm³, ratio 6:1. Cell B: SA = 54 cm², V = 27 cm³, ratio 2:1. Volume grows as the cube.

options.text: Cell B has a higher ratio because it has more total surface area than Cell A
options.explanation: While Cell B has more total surface area, its SA:V ratio is lower because volume increased proportionally more.

options.text: Both have the same ratio because they are the same shape despite different sizes
options.explanation: Same shape does not mean same ratio; larger cells have lower SA:V ratios.

options.text: Cell A has a lower ratio because smaller cells always have less surface area overall
options.explanation: Cell A has less total surface but a higher SA:V ratio, which is what matters for efficiency.

toLevel4.stem: Red blood cells are flat, disc-shaped cells rather than spherical. How does this shape benefit their function?

options.text: The flat shape increases SA:V ratio, improving gas exchange efficiency across the membrane
options.explanation: A flattened shape provides more surface area relative to volume compared to a sphere, enhancing O₂ and CO₂ exchange.

options.text: The flat shape allows them to store more haemoglobin inside their large central cavity
options.explanation: Red blood cells are biconcave to maximise surface area for gas exchange, not to create a storage cavity.

options.text: The flat shape makes them heavier so they sink to the bottom of blood vessels quickly
options.explanation: Being flat does not make them heavier; the shape optimises gas exchange.

options.text: The flat shape protects them from bursting because it reduces internal water pressure
options.explanation: The shape is primarily for maximising the SA:V ratio for gas exchange.

toLevel4.stem: Intestinal epithelial cells have microvilli on their surface. How does this relate to the SA:V ratio concept?

options.text: Microvilli increase the surface area without significantly increasing volume, improving absorption
options.explanation: The finger-like projections greatly increase the membrane surface available for nutrient absorption.

options.text: Microvilli decrease the SA:V ratio to slow down nutrient absorption across the membrane
options.explanation: Microvilli increase, not decrease, the SA:V ratio to enhance absorption.

options.text: Microvilli are purely decorative and have no functional relationship to SA:V ratio at all
options.explanation: Microvilli have a clear functional role in increasing surface area for absorption.

options.text: Microvilli reduce the cell volume to make the cell smaller and easier to replace when worn
options.explanation: Microvilli increase surface area; they do not reduce volume.

toLevel4.stem: An amoeba is relatively large for a single-celled organism but survives because it has an irregular shape with many extensions. How does this help?

options.text: The extensions increase the SA:V ratio, maintaining efficient exchange despite the large size
options.explanation: Pseudopods and irregular extensions increase the surface area relative to volume, improving exchange.

options.text: The extensions allow the amoeba to move faster and catch prey more efficiently in water
options.explanation: While extensions aid movement, they also critically increase the SA:V ratio for exchange.

options.text: The irregular shape reduces the cell's volume so it is actually much smaller than it appears
options.explanation: The extensions add surface area without significantly changing the principle of maintaining exchange.

options.text: The extensions have no effect on SA:V ratio because they are too thin to count as surface
options.explanation: Extensions add significant surface area and directly improve the SA:V ratio.

toLevel4.stem: A student models cells using agar cubes of different sizes soaked in indicator dye. The smallest cube changes colour throughout, while only the outer layer of the largest cube changes. What does this demonstrate?

options.text: Diffusion is sufficient in small cells but cannot reach the centre of large cells quickly
options.explanation: The small cube has a high SA:V ratio so dye reaches the centre; the large cube's low SA:V ratio means the centre remains unaffected.

options.text: The indicator dye only works on small surfaces and is ineffective on larger surfaces
options.explanation: The dye works regardless of size; the issue is that diffusion cannot reach the centre of large cubes.

options.text: Large cubes are made of denser agar that blocks the dye from penetrating to the centre
options.explanation: Both cubes have the same agar density; the difference is due to SA:V ratio and diffusion distance.

options.text: Small cubes absorb dye faster because they have fewer pores for the dye to enter through
options.explanation: Small cubes have a higher SA:V ratio, allowing dye to reach the centre; pore number is not the issue.

toLevel4.stem: Mitochondria have a highly folded inner membrane (cristae). How does this relate to the SA:V ratio concept?

options.text: Folding increases the surface area for reactions without increasing organelle volume
options.explanation: The cristae provide more membrane surface for the electron transport chain within the same volume.

options.text: Folding decreases the surface area to slow down ATP production and conserve energy
options.explanation: Folding increases surface area to maximise ATP production, not decrease it.

options.text: Folding is random and has no functional relationship to the SA:V concept at all
options.explanation: Cristae folding is a direct application of increasing SA:V ratio for functional efficiency.

options.text: Folding increases the volume of the mitochondria to store more glucose for later use
options.explanation: Folding increases surface area, not volume; glucose is not stored in mitochondria.

toLevel4.stem: A student calculates that cutting a cube into 8 equal smaller cubes doubles the total surface area. What effect does this have on SA:V ratio?

options.text: Each smaller cube has a higher SA:V ratio than the original large cube
options.explanation: Dividing the cube increases the SA:V ratio of each piece because the total surface area increases while total volume remains the same.

options.text: The SA:V ratio decreases because there are now more pieces with more total surface
options.explanation: More surface area per unit volume means a higher SA:V ratio, not lower.

options.text: The SA:V ratio remains unchanged because the total volume is still the same overall
options.explanation: While total volume is the same, each individual piece has a higher SA:V ratio.

options.text: The SA:V ratio cannot be calculated for cubes that have been cut into smaller pieces
options.explanation: SA:V ratio can be calculated for any shape; each smaller cube has a measurably higher ratio.

toLevel4.stem: Red blood cells have a {{blank:1}} shape that maximises their SA:V ratio for efficient {{blank:2}} exchange.

options.text: biconcave disc
options.explanation: The flat, indented shape increases surface area relative to volume.

options.text: perfectly spherical
options.explanation: A sphere has the lowest SA:V ratio for a given volume; red blood cells are disc-shaped.

options.text: elongated rod
options.explanation: Red blood cells are biconcave discs, not elongated rods.

options.text: gas
options.explanation: The high SA:V ratio allows efficient exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

options.text: food
options.explanation: Red blood cells transport gases, not food molecules.

options.text: waste
options.explanation: While CO₂ is a waste gas, the primary function is gas exchange (O₂ and CO₂).

toLevel4.stem: Intestinal cells have {{blank:1}} that increase surface area for {{blank:2}} without significantly increasing cell volume.

options.text: microvilli
options.explanation: Microvilli are finger-like projections that greatly increase the membrane surface area.

options.text: flagella
options.explanation: Flagella are for cell movement, not for increasing absorption surface area.

options.text: cilia
options.explanation: Cilia move substances along surfaces; microvilli increase absorption surface area.

options.text: nutrient absorption
options.explanation: More surface area means more membrane for absorbing nutrients from digested food.

options.text: cell division
options.explanation: Microvilli enhance absorption, not cell division.

options.text: waste storage
options.explanation: Microvilli increase absorption capacity, not waste storage.

toLevel4.stem: In the agar cube experiment, the smallest cube changed colour completely because its high {{blank:1}} allowed dye to {{blank:2}} to the centre.

options.text: SA:V ratio
options.explanation: The small cube's high SA:V ratio means the centre is close to the surface, allowing dye to diffuse throughout.

options.text: temperature
options.explanation: Temperature was the same for all cubes; the SA:V ratio explains the difference.

options.text: dye concentration
options.explanation: All cubes were in the same dye concentration; the SA:V ratio is the variable.

options.text: diffuse
options.explanation: The short diffusion distance in a small cube allows dye to reach the centre quickly.

options.text: evaporate
options.explanation: Dye does not evaporate into the cube; it diffuses through the agar.

options.text: crystallise
options.explanation: Dye does not crystallise; it diffuses through the agar from the surface inward.

toLevel5.stem: Some single-celled organisms such as Paramecium are relatively large yet survive without being multicellular. Analyse how their structure compensates for their size.

options.text: They use elongated shapes and internal compartments to maintain effective exchange
options.explanation: Non-spherical shapes and internal organelles increase the effective SA:V ratio, allowing exchange to remain efficient.

options.text: They have no need for exchange because they produce all materials internally by themselves
options.explanation: All cells require exchange of nutrients and wastes with their environment.

options.text: They simply tolerate inefficient exchange because they have very low metabolic demands
options.explanation: Paramecium is metabolically active; its structure compensates for its size through shape adaptations.

options.text: They rely entirely on active transport which is not affected by SA:V ratio limitations
options.explanation: Active transport still occurs at the membrane surface, so SA:V ratio still matters.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that if technology could create a cell with a perfectly efficient membrane, cell size would no longer be limited. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; even a perfect membrane cannot overcome the diffusion distance to a large cell's centre
options.explanation: Regardless of membrane efficiency, substances must still travel from the surface to the interior; diffusion is too slow over large distances.

options.text: Correct; membrane efficiency is the only factor limiting cell size in all organisms
options.explanation: Diffusion distance within the cell is also a critical limitation that membrane efficiency cannot overcome.

options.text: Incorrect; but only because cell size is limited by the amount of DNA in the nucleus
options.explanation: While DNA content matters, the primary size limit is the SA:V ratio and internal diffusion distance.

options.text: Correct; with perfect membranes, cells could grow to any size without any negative consequences
options.explanation: Internal diffusion distance would still limit cell size regardless of membrane efficiency.

toLevel5.stem: Muscle cells are elongated and contain many mitochondria distributed throughout their length. How does this arrangement relate to SA:V ratio principles?

options.text: Distributed mitochondria ensure ATP is produced close to where it is needed, compensating for the long diffusion distance
options.explanation: Spreading mitochondria throughout the cell reduces the effective diffusion distance for ATP, addressing the SA:V challenge of elongated cells.

options.text: Mitochondria are distributed randomly and their position has no functional significance at all
options.explanation: The distribution is functionally significant; it reduces the diffusion distance for ATP delivery.

options.text: Muscle cells have so many mitochondria that SA:V ratio is completely irrelevant to their function
options.explanation: SA:V ratio principles still apply; the distribution of mitochondria is an adaptation to manage this.

options.text: Elongated cells have a higher volume than spherical cells, so they need more mitochondria for size
options.explanation: The elongated shape increases SA:V ratio, and distributed mitochondria reduce internal diffusion distance.

toLevel5.stem: An ostrich egg is one of the largest single cells. Does this contradict the SA:V ratio principle? Evaluate.

options.text: Not really; the egg is mostly yolk storage and has low metabolic activity, reducing exchange demands
options.explanation: The egg's large size is tolerated because it is primarily a nutrient store with minimal metabolic activity, not an actively metabolising cell.

options.text: Yes; the ostrich egg proves that SA:V ratio has no effect on cell size in any organism
options.explanation: The ostrich egg is a special case with low metabolic needs; it does not disprove the SA:V principle.

options.text: Not really; but only because ostrich eggs are not actually single cells in biological terms
options.explanation: Ostrich eggs are single cells; they survive at this size because of their low metabolic demands.

options.text: Yes; all large cells function just as efficiently as small cells regardless of their SA:V ratio
options.explanation: Most large cells would not function efficiently; the ostrich egg is an exception due to its storage function.

toLevel5.stem: A flat leaf has a very different shape from a spherical fruit. How does SA:V ratio explain these different structures?

options.text: The flat leaf maximises SA:V for gas exchange and light capture, while the sphere minimises SA:V for storage
options.explanation: Leaves need high SA:V for CO₂ and O₂ exchange plus light absorption; fruits minimise surface to protect stored sugars.

options.text: Both structures have identical SA:V ratios because they belong to the same organism species
options.explanation: Different shapes produce very different SA:V ratios; the leaf and fruit serve different functions.

options.text: The leaf is flat because it grows faster than the fruit, which grows slowly into a sphere
options.explanation: The shapes are determined by function and SA:V requirements, not growth speed.

options.text: SA:V ratio does not apply to plant structures because plants are multicellular organisms
options.explanation: SA:V ratio principles apply at all levels of biological organisation, including plant organs.

toLevel5.stem: A student suggests that cancer cells grow out of control because they ignore SA:V ratio limits. Evaluate this idea.

options.text: Partially correct; cancer cells divide rapidly but still face SA:V constraints, often developing blood vessel networks to compensate
options.explanation: Tumours stimulate angiogenesis (new blood vessel growth) to supply nutrients, partially compensating for SA:V limitations.

options.text: Completely correct; cancer cells have evolved to be immune to all SA:V ratio limitations entirely
options.explanation: Cancer cells still face SA:V constraints; tumours that cannot develop blood supply die in their centres.

options.text: Completely incorrect; cancer has nothing to do with cell division or SA:V ratio principles at all
options.explanation: Cancer involves uncontrolled division, and tumours do face SA:V limitations that affect their growth.

options.text: Partially correct; but cancer cells solve this by becoming smaller than normal cells permanently
options.explanation: Cancer cells do not necessarily become smaller; they recruit blood vessels to overcome SA:V constraints.

toLevel5.stem: Elephant cells and mouse cells are approximately the same size, despite the animals being vastly different in body size. What explains this?

options.text: Cell size is constrained by SA:V ratio; elephants simply have far more cells than mice
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio limits how large individual cells can be, so larger organisms achieve their size by having more cells, not bigger ones.

options.text: Elephant cells are actually much larger than mouse cells but appear the same under a microscope
options.explanation: Cell sizes are genuinely similar across most mammals; larger body size comes from more cells.

options.text: Mice have fewer but larger cells while elephants have many smaller cells packed tightly together
options.explanation: Both have similarly sized cells; the elephant simply has far more of them.

options.text: SA:V ratio only applies to single-celled organisms and has no relevance to animal cell sizes
options.explanation: SA:V ratio constrains cell size in all organisms, including animal cells.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes that nanotechnology could create artificial organelles to increase a cell's internal exchange surface. Evaluate whether this could allow cells to grow larger.

options.text: It could help by creating internal exchange surfaces, similar to how organelles naturally increase internal SA:V
options.explanation: Just as cristae and ER increase internal surface area, artificial structures could potentially improve exchange within a larger cell.

options.text: It would have no effect because cell size is fixed by genetics and cannot be altered by technology
options.explanation: Cell size is limited by physics (SA:V ratio), not just genetics; addressing the physical constraint could theoretically allow larger cells.

options.text: It would cause cells to shrink because additional organelles would take up too much internal space
options.explanation: The goal is to increase internal exchange surfaces, not to fill the cell; the concept is analogous to natural organelle function.

options.text: It would be impossible because no artificial structure can replicate the function of biological membranes
options.explanation: While challenging, the principle of increasing internal surface area is sound and mirrors existing biological strategies.

toLevel5.stem: Elephant cells and mouse cells are similar in size because cell size is limited by the {{blank:1}}; elephants achieve larger body size by having {{blank:2}} cells.

options.text: SA:V ratio
options.explanation: The SA:V ratio constrains individual cell size regardless of organism body size.

options.text: DNA length
options.explanation: While DNA content can affect cell size, the SA:V ratio is the primary physical constraint.

options.text: body temperature
options.explanation: Body temperature does not directly limit cell size; the SA:V ratio does.

options.text: more
options.explanation: Larger organisms have more cells, not bigger cells, to achieve their body size.

options.text: fewer
options.explanation: Elephants have far more cells than mice, not fewer.

options.text: identical
options.explanation: Elephants have many more cells than mice despite similar individual cell sizes.

toLevel5.stem: Even with a perfect membrane, cell size would still be limited because {{blank:1}} inside the cell becomes too slow over large {{blank:2}}.

options.text: diffusion
options.explanation: Substances must diffuse from the membrane to the cell interior; this becomes too slow in very large cells.

options.text: osmosis
options.explanation: While osmosis involves water, the general limitation is diffusion of all substances to the cell interior.

options.text: photosynthesis
options.explanation: Photosynthesis is a metabolic process, not the factor limiting internal transport in all cells.

options.text: distances
options.explanation: The distance from the membrane to the centre of a large cell is too great for diffusion to be effective.

options.text: temperatures
options.explanation: Temperature affects diffusion rate but is not the primary limiting factor related to cell size.

options.text: time periods
options.explanation: The issue is spatial distance, not time; substances cannot reach the centre quickly enough.
